title: Choosing a fire site
def: A safe fire site is on bare mineral soil, clear of overhanging branches, dry grass, and roots, and downwind from your shelter.
look: bare soil or sand, or an existing ring
a cleared circle about 10 feet (3 m) wide
water nearby to put it out
use: Scrape away leaves and duff to bare soil, build a ring of rocks, keep water or a shovel at hand, and keep it small. Check local rules first.
not: Do not build under low branches, on peat or roots, or on dry grass in wind.

title: Tinder, kindling, and fuel
def: Tinder is fine dry material that catches a spark, kindling is pencil-sized sticks that carry the flame, and fuel is the larger wood that burns for hours.
look: tinder: birch bark, fatwood shavings, dry grass, cattail fluff, cotton with petroleum jelly
kindling: dry twigs from pencil lead to thumb thick
fuel: wrist-thick and larger dead dry wood
use: Gather three piles before you light: a double handful of tinder, twice as much kindling, and plenty of fuel. Use dead, standing, dry wood, which snaps when it is dry.
not: Do not use damp wood, treated lumber, or trash.
region: Birch bark and eastern white pine fatwood from dead stumps are classic New England tinder; check the rules on what you may take.

title: Building and lighting a basic fire (teepee)
def: A teepee fire is a cone of kindling leaned over a nest of tinder, lit from the windward side so the flame climbs.
look: tinder bundle in the center
kindling leaning inward like a tent
fuel stacked nearby
use: Place the tinder bundle, lean kindling around it, leave a gap on the windward side, light the tinder, and add small fuel as it catches. Blow gently at the base and add bigger pieces slowly.
not: Do not smother the flame with too much fuel too early.
steps: Clear a bare spot and ring it with rocks.
Place a handful of tinder in the center.
Lean kindling over it in a teepee with an opening to light.
Light the tinder from the upwind side.
Add bigger sticks as the fire grows.
call: Keep water nearby and never leave a fire unattended.

title: Starting a fire in rain or with wet wood
def: In rain, use dry material from under cover: dead branches still on trees, inner bark, and shaved wood, and protect the flame under a tarp.
look: dead lower branches that snap
split wet logs to reach dry centers
fatwood or a dry starter you carried
use: Look for dry tinder under logs and evergreen boughs, split wood to reach its dry inside, and shave fine curls. Build on a platform of sticks in snow or wet ground and shield the fire from rain.
not: Do not use wet bark or green wood, and do not light in a closed shelter.

title: Starting a fire in snow
also: build a platform for a fire
def: A fire in snow needs a platform of green logs or stones so it does not sink and go out.
look: a platform of green logs, flat rocks, or a layer of sticks
a windbreak
dry tinder you kept inside your jacket
use: Stamp down the snow, lay a log platform, and build the fire on top. Keep dry tinder against your body, and feed it slowly.
not: Do not build under a snow-laden branch that can fall onto the fire.

title: Putting a fire out completely
def: A fire is out only when the ashes are cold to the touch; drown it, stir it, and drown it again.
look: steam or hissing means it is still hot
no glowing embers
back of your hand feels no heat
use: Let the fire burn down, pour water on the embers, stir the ashes and soil with a stick, and add more water until nothing hisses. Feel for heat with the back of your hand.
not: Do not just bury a hot fire or leave it smoldering, and do not leave until it is cold.
call: Call 911 if a fire gets away from you.

title: Camp stove versus open fire
def: A camp stove is more controlled and leaves less trace than an open fire, but any stove, grill, or charcoal burner must never be used indoors, in a tent, or in a garage.
look: stoves burn liquid or gas fuel
charcoal makes carbon monoxide
fuel should be stored away from heat
use: Cook outdoors on a stable, flat surface, away from tents and dry grass, and have water handy. Let it cool before refueling.
not: Do not use a camp stove, grill, or generator in a house, garage, or tent.
call: Get out into fresh air for headache or dizziness; call 911 for carbon monoxide symptoms.

title: Is a fire legal here? Fire bans and permits
def: Fire rules vary by state, town, and land, and bans are common in dry or windy weather, so check the official source before you light one.
look: a burn ban or a red flag warning
state, town, or land-manager rules
a campfire permit requirement
use: Check with the local fire department, the state forest service, or the land manager, and follow any ban. If fires are banned, use a stove only if rules allow.
not: Do not guess; do not light a fire during a ban.
region: Check the Maine Forest Service, your state forestry office, and the town for burn permits and bans.

title: What not to burn
def: Never burn poison ivy, treated lumber, painted wood, plastic, or trash; the smoke is toxic.
look: poison ivy smoke carries irritating oil
treated lumber has chemicals
plastics make toxic fumes
use: Burn only clean, dry, untreated wood. Pack out trash.
not: Do not burn poison ivy, pressure-treated wood, or plastics, and do not breathe the smoke.
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing after smoke exposure.

title: Smoke, wind, and where to sit
def: Smoke drifts downwind, so sit upwind or to the side, and dry wood burns cleaner.
look: smoke blowing toward your seat
a smoky fire from wet wood
wind shifts
use: Move your seat upwind, burn dry wood, and keep the fire small. If it keeps smoking, stir and add dry fuel.
not: Do not sit in the smoke or breathe it for long.

title: Signal fire
def: A signal fire is a fire built to be seen from a distance, with green boughs for white smoke by day and bright fuel at night.
look: three fires in a triangle is a distress signal
green leaves make dense smoke
a clearing for visibility
use: Build it on an open spot, keep tinder dry and ready, and light it when an aircraft or searchers are close. Add green boughs for smoke by day.
not: Do not leave it unattended or start it near dry grass.

title: Ferro rod, matches, and lighters
also: how to use a ferro rod
def: A ferrocerium rod throws hot sparks when scraped, and it works wet; matches and lighters are easier but fail when wet or empty.
look: scrape the rod down with a sharp spine, keeping it close to the tinder
carry two ways to light
a lighter kept dry in a pocket
use: Hold the rod near the tinder and pull the striker backward fast. Carry a lighter, matches in a waterproof case, and a ferro rod as a backup.
not: Do not rely on one ignition source, and do not use a bow drill until all else fails.

title: Keeping and moving an ember
def: A viable ember is glowing red and spreads when you blow on it; a dead ember is black and cool.
look: a bright orange glow when blown on
char cloth or punky wood catches a spark
an ember in dry tinder can be blown into flame
use: Place the ember in a nest of fine tinder, fold the tinder around it, and blow gently until it flames. Bank a fire at night with large logs and ash.
not: Do not leave a fire banked unattended in wind.
